cards.prompt:
When your [[browser]] asks for a page, the request travels like a letter inside envelopes inside a parcel. Each wrapper follows its own set of rules, a **protocol**, with one job.

Put them in order, from the **letter in the middle** at the top to the **outside wrapper** at the bottom.

items.label: HTTP: the request for the page
TCP: gets it to the right program, reliably
IP: addresses to reach the right computer
Wi-Fi or Ethernet (wired): carries it to the next device

cards.explanation: The **HTTP** request is the letter at the centre. **TCP** wraps it so it reaches the right program reliably, **IP** wraps that so it reaches the right computer, and **Wi-Fi or Ethernet** carries the whole bundle one step at a time. At the other end, the wrappers come off in reverse: the outside first, the letter last.
cards.hint: The request itself is the letter. The outside wrapper is whatever physically carries the bundle to the next device.
cards.nudge: Each wrapper goes around everything before it. Start with what the browser actually wants to say, then add the program, the computer and the next device.

cards.title: How strangers understand each other
cards.body:
Your phone, your [[router]] and a website's [[server]] were made by different companies, yet they understand each other perfectly. They all follow the same **protocols**: rules for what each message looks like, what order messages go in, and what to do when something goes wrong.

The rules are published free, so anyone can build something that works with everything else.

cards.prompt:
Every job online has its own protocol. **HTTPS** fetches web pages securely. **DNS** turns names into addresses. **SMTP** and **IMAP** handle email.

Which protocol does each job?

items.label: Logging in to your bank's website
Checking your inbox on a new phone

cards.explanation: Web pages come with **HTTPS**. Looking up names is **DNS**'s job, and that includes finding where a domain's email goes: its MX record. Sending and reading email use the email protocols, **SMTP** and **IMAP**. The tricky one is "where example.org's email goes": it's about email, but it's a lookup, so it's DNS.
cards.hint: Ask what each job really is: fetching a page, looking something up, or moving or reading an email?
cards.nudge: Check the email-sounding jobs. Finding **where** a domain's email should go is a lookup, not sending or reading mail.

cards.prompt:
Email uses two protocols. **SMTP** sends mail on its way, from your app to your provider and between mail [[servers|server]]. **IMAP** lets an app read mail that's kept on a server.

You email `hello@example.org`. Put the email's journey in order.

items.label: You press Send in your email app
Your app sends it with SMTP to your provider's mail server
Your provider looks up example.org's MX record with DNS
Your provider delivers it with SMTP to example.org's mail server
The recipient's app fetches it with IMAP

cards.explanation: SMTP carries the email **twice**: from your app to your provider, then from server to server. In between, DNS's **MX record** says where example.org's email goes. Finally, the recipient reads it with **IMAP**. One email, three protocols!
cards.hint: SMTP carries the email twice. Before the second trip, your provider must find out where example.org's mail should go.
cards.nudge: Reading with IMAP only happens once the email has arrived. And your provider can't deliver it until it knows where to send it.

cards.prompt: Ana reads an email in her phone's email app, then opens the email app on her laptop. The same email is already there, marked as read. Which protocol makes that possible?

options.text: IMAP, because her mail stays on the server for every app
SMTP, because it copies each email onto every device she owns
options.nudge: SMTP's job is sending mail on its way. Think about where the email is kept while Ana reads it on two devices.

options.text: DNS, because it looks up which of her devices has the email
options.nudge: DNS turns names into addresses, like where a domain's email goes. It doesn't keep track of what Ana has read.

options.text: HTTPS, because her inbox is really just a secure web page
options.nudge: Her email app isn't fetching a web page here. Think about the protocol for reading mail kept on a server.

cards.explanation: With **IMAP**, the email stays on her provider's [[server]], and each app reads it from there. So her phone and laptop see the same inbox, read marks and all. SMTP only sends mail on its way, and DNS only looks things up. (If Ana used her provider's website instead, that would be HTTPS, but here she uses email apps.)
cards.hint: Where is the email kept while Ana reads it on two devices? Which protocol reads mail from there?

cards.prompt: A developer runs a website at `http://example.com:8080`, not on the usual port 80. How can that work?

options.text: Port 80 is a custom, not a law: the `:8080` says which door
8080 is how 80 is written in hex, so it's really the same port
options.nudge: 80 and 8080 are different port numbers, and hex has nothing to do with it. Think about what the `:8080` in the address tells the browser.

options.text: Browsers try every port in turn until one of them answers
options.nudge: Browsers don't guess. Look at the address again: it already contains the information the browser needs.

options.text: All ports above 1,024 are kept for websites, so any of them works
options.nudge: Websites can use lots of different ports. Think about what the `:8080` in the address is doing.

cards.explanation: Standard port numbers are an **agreement** (part of the shared rules), so nobody has to ask where to knock. A web [[server]] can listen on any free [[port]], and the `:8080` in the address tells the browser which one to use. Browsers don't guess ports, and high port numbers aren't kept for websites.
cards.hint: Think about why standard ports exist: so everyone knows where to knock. Is that a rule computers must obey, or an agreement?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **protocol** is a shared set of rules for one job.
- Protocols wrap like envelopes: [[HTTP]] inside [[TCP]] inside IP.
- Email: **SMTP** sends it, **IMAP** reads it.

Take the quiz to unlock the final module: The Web.
